15	     Purpose: To examine the dose–response of the Nordic hamstring exercise (NHE) on biceps femoris long head (BFlh) architecture
16	     and eccentric knee ﬂexor strength. Design: Randomized interventional trial. Methods: Forty recreationally active males
17	     completed a 6-week NHE training program consisting of either intermittent low volumes (group 1; n = 10), low volumes (group
18	     2; n = 10), initial high volumes followed by low volumes (group 3; n = 10), or progressively increasing volumes (group 4; n = 10).
19	     A 4-week detraining period followed each program. Muscle architecture was assessed weekly during training and after 2 and
20	     4 weeks of detraining. Eccentric knee ﬂexor strength was assessed preintervention and postintervention and after 2 and 4 weeks
21	     of detraining. Results: Following 6 weeks of training, BFlh fascicle length (FL) increased in group 3 (mean difference = 0.83 cm,
22	     d = 0.45, P = .027, +7%) and group 4 (mean difference = 1.48 cm, d = 0.94, P = .004, +14%). FL returned to baseline following
23	     detraining in groups 3 and 4. Strength increased in group 2 (mean difference = 53.6 N, d = 0.55, P = .002, +14%), group 3 (mean
24	     difference = 63.4 N, d = 0.72, P = .027, +17%), and group 4 (mean difference = 74.7, d = 0.83, P = .006, +19%) following
25	     training. Strength returned to baseline following detraining in groups 2 and 3 but not in group 4. Conclusions: Initial high
26	     volumes of the NHE followed by lower volumes, as well as progressively increasing volumes, can elicit increases in BFlh FL and
27	     eccentric knee ﬂexor strength. Low volumes of the NHE were insufﬁcient to increase FL, although as few as 48 repetitions in 6
28	     weeks did increase strength.

 The Dose–Response of the Nordic Hamstring Exercise on Biceps
    Femoris Architecture and Eccentric Knee Flexor Strength:
               A Randomized Interventional Trial
                           Fearghal P. Behan, Robin Vermeulen, Rod Whiteley, Ryan G. Timmins,
                                           Joshua D. Ruddy, and David A. Opar

     Purpose: To examine the dose–response of the Nordic hamstring exercise (NHE) on biceps femoris long head (BFlh) architecture
     and eccentric knee ﬂexor strength. Design: Randomized interventional trial. Methods: Forty recreationally active males
     completed a 6-week NHE training program consisting of either intermittent low volumes (group 1; n = 10), low volumes (group
     2; n = 10), initial high volumes followed by low volumes (group 3; n = 10), or progressively increasing volumes (group 4; n = 10).
     A 4-week detraining period followed each program. Muscle architecture was assessed weekly during training and after 2 and
     4 weeks of detraining. Eccentric knee ﬂexor strength was assessed preintervention and postintervention and after 2 and 4 weeks
     of detraining. Results: Following 6 weeks of training, BFlh fascicle length (FL) increased in group 3 (mean difference = 0.83 cm,
     d = 0.45, P = .027, +7%) and group 4 (mean difference = 1.48 cm, d = 0.94, P = .004, +14%). FL returned to baseline following
     detraining in groups 3 and 4. Strength increased in group 2 (mean difference = 53.6 N, d = 0.55, P = .002, +14%), group 3 (mean
     difference = 63.4 N, d = 0.72, P = .027, +17%), and group 4 (mean difference = 74.7, d = 0.83, P = .006, +19%) following
     training. Strength returned to baseline following detraining in groups 2 and 3 but not in group 4. Conclusions: Initial high
     volumes of the NHE followed by lower volumes, as well as progressively increasing volumes, can elicit increases in BFlh FL and
     eccentric knee ﬂexor strength. Low volumes of the NHE were insufﬁcient to increase FL, although as few as 48 repetitions in 6
     weeks did increase strength.

     Keywords: eccentric training, fascicle length, muscle architecture, ultrasound

9	on Eccentric Strength and Muscle Architecture Adaptations:
10	A Systematic Review and Meta‑analyses
11	Matthew Cuthbert1,2           · Nicholas Ripley1 · John J. McMahon1 · Martin Evans2 · G. Gregory Haff1,3 · Paul Comfort1,4
12	
13	
14	© The Author(s) 2019

16	
17	Abstract
18	Background Although performance of the Nordic hamstring exercise (NHE) has been shown to elicit adaptations that may
19	reduce hamstring strain injury (HSI) risk and occurrence, compliance in NHE interventions in professional soccer teams is
20	low despite a high occurrence of HSI in soccer. A possible reason for low compliance is the high dosages prescribed within
21	the recommended interventions. The aim of this review was to investigate the effect of NHE-training volume on eccentric
22	hamstring strength and biceps femoris fascicle length adaptations.
23	Methods A literature search was conducted using the SPORTDiscus, Ovid, and PubMed databases. A total of 293 stud-
24	ies were identified prior to application of the following inclusion criteria: (1) a minimum of 4 weeks of NHE training was
25	completed; (2) mean ± standard deviation (SD) pre- and post-intervention were provided for the measured variables to allow
26	for secondary analysis; and (3) biceps femoris muscle architecture was measured, which resulted in 13 studies identified
27	for further analysis. The TESTEX criteria were used to assess the quality of studies with risk of bias assessment assessed
28	using a fail-safe N (Rosenthal method). Consistency of studies was analysed using I2 as a test of heterogeneity and second-
29	ary analysis of studies included Hedges’ g effect sizes for strength and muscle architecture variables to provide comparison
30	within studies, between-study differences were estimated using a random-effects model.
31	Results A range of scores (3–11 out of 15) from the TESTEX criteria were reported, showing variation in study quality. A
32	‘low risk of bias’ was observed in the randomized controlled trials included, with no study bias shown for both strength or
33	architecture (N = 250 and 663, respectively; p < 0.001). Study consistency was moderate to high for strength (I2 = 62.49%)
34	and muscle architecture (I2 = 88.03%). Within-study differences showed that following interventions of ≥ 6 weeks, very
35	large positive effect sizes were seen in eccentric strength following both high volume (g = 2.12) and low volume (g = 2.28)
36	NHE interventions. Similar results were reported for changes in fascicle length (g ≥ 2.58) and a large-to-very large positive
37	reduction in pennation angle (g ≥ 1.31). Between-study differences were estimated to be at a magnitude of 0.374 (p = 0.009)
38	for strength and 0.793 (p < 0.001) for architecture.
39	Conclusions Reducing NHE volume prescription does not negatively affect adaptations in eccentric strength and muscle
40	architecture when compared with high dose interventions. These findings suggest that lower volumes of NHE may be more
41	appropriate for athletes, with an aim to increase intervention compliance, potentially reducing the risk of HSI.

    SYSTEMATIC REVIEW



The Effect of Nordic Hamstring Exercise Intervention Volume
on Eccentric Strength and Muscle Architecture Adaptations:
A Systematic Review and Meta‑analyses
Matthew Cuthbert1,2           · Nicholas Ripley1 · John J. McMahon1 · Martin Evans2 · G. Gregory Haff1,3 · Paul Comfort1,4


© The Author(s) 2019


Abstract
Background Although performance of the Nordic hamstring exercise (NHE) has been shown to elicit adaptations that may
reduce hamstring strain injury (HSI) risk and occurrence, compliance in NHE interventions in professional soccer teams is
low despite a high occurrence of HSI in soccer. A possible reason for low compliance is the high dosages prescribed within
the recommended interventions. The aim of this review was to investigate the effect of NHE-training volume on eccentric
hamstring strength and biceps femoris fascicle length adaptations.
Methods A literature search was conducted using the SPORTDiscus, Ovid, and PubMed databases. A total of 293 stud-
ies were identified prior to application of the following inclusion criteria: (1) a minimum of 4 weeks of NHE training was
completed; (2) mean ± standard deviation (SD) pre- and post-intervention were provided for the measured variables to allow
for secondary analysis; and (3) biceps femoris muscle architecture was measured, which resulted in 13 studies identified
for further analysis. The TESTEX criteria were used to assess the quality of studies with risk of bias assessment assessed
using a fail-safe N (Rosenthal method). Consistency of studies was analysed using I2 as a test of heterogeneity and second-
ary analysis of studies included Hedges’ g effect sizes for strength and muscle architecture variables to provide comparison
within studies, between-study differences were estimated using a random-effects model.
Results A range of scores (3–11 out of 15) from the TESTEX criteria were reported, showing variation in study quality. A
‘low risk of bias’ was observed in the randomized controlled trials included, with no study bias shown for both strength or
architecture (N = 250 and 663, respectively; p < 0.001). Study consistency was moderate to high for strength (I2 = 62.49%)
and muscle architecture (I2 = 88.03%). Within-study differences showed that following interventions of ≥ 6 weeks, very
large positive effect sizes were seen in eccentric strength following both high volume (g = 2.12) and low volume (g = 2.28)
NHE interventions. Similar results were reported for changes in fascicle length (g ≥ 2.58) and a large-to-very large positive
reduction in pennation angle (g ≥ 1.31). Between-study differences were estimated to be at a magnitude of 0.374 (p = 0.009)
for strength and 0.793 (p < 0.001) for architecture.
Conclusions Reducing NHE volume prescription does not negatively affect adaptations in eccentric strength and muscle
architecture when compared with high dose interventions. These findings suggest that lower volumes of NHE may be more
appropriate for athletes, with an aim to increase intervention compliance, potentially reducing the risk of HSI.

8	The Effectiveness of Resisted Sled Training (RST) for Sprint
9	Performance: A Systematic Review and Meta‑analysis
10	Pedro E. Alcaraz1,2 · Jorge Carlos‑Vivas1 · Bruno O. Oponjuru1 · Alejandro Martínez‑Rodríguez3
11	
12	
13	© Springer International Publishing AG, part of Springer Nature 2018
14	
15	
16	Abstract
17	Background Sprinting is key in the development and final results of competitions in a range of sport disciplines, both indi-
18	vidual (e.g., athletics) and team sports. Resisted sled training (RST) might provide an effective training method to improve
19	sprinting, in both the acceleration and the maximum-velocity phases. However, substantial discrepancies exist in the lit-
20	erature regarding the influence of training status and sled load prescription in relation to the specific components of sprint
21	performance to be developed and the phase of sprint.
22	Objectives Our objectives were to review the state of the current literature on intervention studies that have analyzed the
23	effects of RST on sprint performance in both the acceleration and the maximum-velocity phases in healthy athletes and to
24	establish which RST load characteristics produce the largest improvements in sprint performance.
25	Methods We performed a literature search in PubMed, SPORTDiscus, and Web of Science up to and including 9 January
26	2018. Peer-reviewed studies were included if they met all the following eligibility criteria: (1) published in a scientific jour-
27	nal; (2) original experimental and longitudinal study; (3) participants were at least recreationally active and towed or pulled
28	the sled while running at maximum intensity; (4) RST was one of the main training methods used; (5) studies identified the
29	load of the sled, distance covered, and sprint time and/or sprint velocity for both baseline and post-training results; (6) sprint
30	performance was measured using timing gates, radar gun, or stopwatch; (7) published in the English language; and (8) had
31	a quality assessment score > 6 points.
32	Results A total of 2376 articles were found. After filtering procedures, only 13 studies were included in this meta-analysis.
33	In the included studies, 32 RST groups and 15 control groups were analyzed for sprint time in the different phases and full
34	sprint. Significant improvements were found between baseline and post-training in sprint performance in the acceleration
35	phase (effect size [ES] 0.61; p = 0.0001; standardized mean difference [SMD] 0.57; 95% confidence interval [CI] − 0.85 to
36	− 0.28) and full sprint (ES 0.36; p = 0.009; SMD 0.38; 95% CI − 0.67 to − 0.10). However, non-significant improvements
37	were observed between pre- and post-test in sprint time in the maximum-velocity phase (ES 0.27; p = 0.25; SMD 0.18; 95%
38	CI − 0.49 to 0.13). Furthermore, studies that included a control group found a non-significant improvement in participants
39	in the RST group compared with the control group, independent of the analyzed phase.
40	Conclusions RST is an effective method to improve sprint performance, specifically in the early acceleration phase. However,
41	it cannot be said that this method is more effective than the same training without overload. The effect of RST is greatest in
42	recreationally active or trained men who practice team sports such as football or rugby. Moreover, the intensity (load) is not
43	a determinant of sprint performance improvement, but the recommended volume is > 160 m per session, and approximately
44	2680 m per week, with a training frequency of two to three times per week, for at least 6 weeks. Finally, rigid surfaces appear
45	to enhance the effect of RST on sprint performance.

 SYSTEMATIC REVIEW



The Effectiveness of Resisted Sled Training (RST) for Sprint
Performance: A Systematic Review and Meta‑analysis
Pedro E. Alcaraz1,2 · Jorge Carlos‑Vivas1 · Bruno O. Oponjuru1 · Alejandro Martínez‑Rodríguez3


© Springer International Publishing AG, part of Springer Nature 2018


Abstract
Background Sprinting is key in the development and final results of competitions in a range of sport disciplines, both indi-
vidual (e.g., athletics) and team sports. Resisted sled training (RST) might provide an effective training method to improve
sprinting, in both the acceleration and the maximum-velocity phases. However, substantial discrepancies exist in the lit-
erature regarding the influence of training status and sled load prescription in relation to the specific components of sprint
performance to be developed and the phase of sprint.
Objectives Our objectives were to review the state of the current literature on intervention studies that have analyzed the
effects of RST on sprint performance in both the acceleration and the maximum-velocity phases in healthy athletes and to
establish which RST load characteristics produce the largest improvements in sprint performance.
Methods We performed a literature search in PubMed, SPORTDiscus, and Web of Science up to and including 9 January
2018. Peer-reviewed studies were included if they met all the following eligibility criteria: (1) published in a scientific jour-
nal; (2) original experimental and longitudinal study; (3) participants were at least recreationally active and towed or pulled
the sled while running at maximum intensity; (4) RST was one of the main training methods used; (5) studies identified the
load of the sled, distance covered, and sprint time and/or sprint velocity for both baseline and post-training results; (6) sprint
performance was measured using timing gates, radar gun, or stopwatch; (7) published in the English language; and (8) had
a quality assessment score > 6 points.
Results A total of 2376 articles were found. After filtering procedures, only 13 studies were included in this meta-analysis.
In the included studies, 32 RST groups and 15 control groups were analyzed for sprint time in the different phases and full
sprint. Significant improvements were found between baseline and post-training in sprint performance in the acceleration
phase (effect size [ES] 0.61; p = 0.0001; standardized mean difference [SMD] 0.57; 95% confidence interval [CI] − 0.85 to
− 0.28) and full sprint (ES 0.36; p = 0.009; SMD 0.38; 95% CI − 0.67 to − 0.10). However, non-significant improvements
were observed between pre- and post-test in sprint time in the maximum-velocity phase (ES 0.27; p = 0.25; SMD 0.18; 95%
CI − 0.49 to 0.13). Furthermore, studies that included a control group found a non-significant improvement in participants
in the RST group compared with the control group, independent of the analyzed phase.
Conclusions RST is an effective method to improve sprint performance, specifically in the early acceleration phase. However,
it cannot be said that this method is more effective than the same training without overload. The effect of RST is greatest in
recreationally active or trained men who practice team sports such as football or rugby. Moreover, the intensity (load) is not
a determinant of sprint performance improvement, but the recommended volume is > 160 m per session, and approximately
2680 m per week, with a training frequency of two to three times per week, for at least 6 weeks. Finally, rigid surfaces appear
to enhance the effect of RST on sprint performance.

{
 "id": "Q76",
 "sourceFile": "PLACEHOLDER",
 "decision": "INCLUDE",
 "exclusionReason": "",
 "degradedReason": "",
 "doiMissing": false,
 "identityCheck": "Title in text 'The Dose-Response Relationship of Exercise-Based Injury Prevention Programmes: Implications for Research and Practice' matches the filename; the article's own DOI is printed on the first page.",
 "confidence": "medium",
 "studyDesign": "Narrative Review",
 "primaryDomain": "Sports Medicine & Injury",
 "domains": ["Sports Medicine & Injury", "Training & Performance"],
 "audiences": ["Sports Medicine", "Athletic Training", "Coaching", "Research & Analytics"],
 "sports": ["Mixed / General Sport"],
 "populations": ["Mixed / Unspecified"],
 "evidenceSummary": "A Current Opinion in Sports Medicine on the dose-response relationship of exercise-based injury prevention programmes (EIPPs), with the duration of practice as the dose and injury rates as the response. The authors screened the sports RCTs in six recent systematic reviews (36 studies after de-duplication) and found that 33 (92%) handled dilution, re-injury and interaction effects in no way. They re-present two analysis approaches on one previously published athletics RCT, where the odds ratio for weekly injury prevalence moved from 0.85 (0.67-1.09) in the primary analysis to 0.28 (0.16-0.48) with the exclusion approach.",
 "screeningLimitations": "The literature screen was non-systematic and the numerical examples come from the authors' own re-analysis of one athletics trial, which they say needs replication. No pooled estimate of the EIPP dose-response is given.",
 "synthesisCaution": "Staff could take the 0.28 odds ratio as the true effect of a prevention programme, when it is one trial re-analysed under an approach the authors themselves say needs validation.",
 "paper": {
   "year": 2025,
   "citation": "Iatropoulos S, Dandrieux PE, Navarro L, Blanco D, Edouard P. The Dose-Response Relationship of Exercise-Based Injury Prevention Programmes: Implications for Research and Practice. Sports Medicine. 2025.",
   "doi": "10.1007/s40279-025-02298-z",
   "abstract": "Exercise-based injury prevention programmes need a period of consistent practice before they reduce injury risk. The authors explain the dose-response concept from pharmacology, show that most RCTs analyse injuries from the first day of the programme, and illustrate two statistical approaches that remove early injuries from the analysis.",
   "tldr": "Injury prevention programmes take weeks to work, so analysing injuries from day one can hide their effect. Plan start dates well before the period when protection is needed.",
   "methods": "Narrative Current Opinion. The authors outline dose-response concepts, screen the sport RCTs in six recent systematic reviews without a systematic search protocol, and re-analyse one earlier athletics RCT using two approaches.",
   "findings": "Of 36 screened RCTs, 33 (92%) did not account for dilution, re-injury or interaction effects, and three accounted for dilution only. In the athletics example, the odds ratio for weekly injury prevalence was 0.85 (0.67-1.09) in the primary analysis, 0.75 (0.56-1.01) after excluding the early period, 0.37 (0.25-0.55) with the inclusion approach and 0.28 (0.16-0.48) with the exclusion approach. The authors estimate that about 6 weeks were needed before this programme reached full effect. In the van der Horst Nordic hamstring trial, cited by the authors, the prevalence reduction was 67% for weeks 14-52 but 56% over the full 52 weeks.",
   "limitations": "The authors call the approaches promising but untested in other RCTs, and the screen was not systematic. Most worked examples come from a single trial.",
   "practicalImplications": "Start a prevention block several weeks before the period it should protect. Do not judge a programme by injuries that occur in its first weeks, and keep athletes on the programme after an early injury.",
   "athleteDev": "Start the injury prevention block several weeks before the competition period it is meant to protect, and keep training through an early injury, because the programme is still building its effect. This is a planning point, not a training-adaptation finding.",
   "rtp": "Not a return-to-sport study. It does not test rehabilitation, return criteria or re-injury after return, so it cannot set return-to-play timelines; the timing point applies only to prevention programmes."
 }
}

   "tldr": "In recreationally active men, a high-volume start followed by low volume, or steadily rising volume, increased hamstring fascicle length and eccentric strength over 6 weeks. input.content:
{
 "id": "Q78",
 "sourceFile": "PLACEHOLDER",
 "decision": "INCLUDE",
 "exclusionReason": "",
 "degradedReason": "",
 "doiMissing": false,
 "identityCheck": "Title in text 'The Effect of Nordic Hamstring Exercise Intervention Volume on Eccentric Strength and Muscle Architecture Adaptations: A Systematic Review and Meta-analyses' matches the filename; the article's own DOI is printed on the first page.",
 "confidence": "high",
 "studyDesign": "Systematic Review / Meta-analysis",
 "primaryDomain": "Training & Performance",
 "domains": ["Training & Performance", "Sports Medicine & Injury"],
 "audiences": ["Performance", "Sports Medicine", "Athletic Training", "Research & Analytics"],
 "sports": ["Mixed / General Sport", "Soccer", "Rugby"],
 "populations": ["Mixed / Unspecified"],
 "evidenceSummary": "A PRISMA-guided systematic review and meta-analysis of 13 NHE training studies (searched in SPORTDiscus, Ovid and PubMed) that measured eccentric strength or biceps femoris architecture after at least 4 weeks. Pooled within-study pre-post effects were very large for eccentric strength after 6 or more weeks with both high-volume (g = 2.12) and low-volume (g = 2.28) protocols, and very large for fascicle length (g of 2.58 or more), with pennation angle falling by a large to very large amount (g of 1.31 or more).",
 "screeningLimitations": "The effects are pre-post changes within each study, not tested comparisons between high and low volume, and study quality was low to moderate (TESTEX 3 to 11 of 15, mean 6) with high heterogeneity (I2 = 62% for strength, 88% for architecture). No protocol was pre-registered, and most studies did not report compliance.",
 "synthesisCaution": "Staff could read the large within-study gains as proof that low-volume NHE works as well as high-volume NHE, but the review did not statistically compare volumes.",
 "paper": {
   "year": 2019,
   "citation": "Cuthbert M, Ripley N, McMahon JJ, Evans M, Haff GG, Comfort P. The Effect of Nordic Hamstring Exercise Intervention Volume on Eccentric Strength and Muscle Architecture Adaptations: A Systematic Review and Meta-analyses. Sports Medicine. 2019.",
   "doi": "10.1007/s40279-019-01178-7",
   "abstract": "Systematic review and meta-analysis of 13 studies on how Nordic hamstring exercise (NHE) training volume relates to eccentric hamstring strength and biceps femoris architecture. Pre-post effects were large across high and low volumes after 6 or more weeks, and volume alone did not show a clear trend.",
   "tldr": "Across studies, NHE protocols of 6 or more weeks produced large strength and fascicle gains at both high and low volumes. Lower, consistent volumes may suit squads where soreness limits compliance.",
   "methods": "PRISMA-guided search of three databases (293 records) to December 2018; 13 studies with at least 4 weeks of NHE and pre-post data on biceps femoris architecture were included. Study quality was rated with TESTEX and risk of bias with the Cochrane tool for the RCTs; pooled Hedges' g values came from random-effects models.",
   "findings": "Eccentric strength and fascicle length showed very large within-study gains after 6 or more weeks at high (g = 2.12) and low (g = 2.28) volumes, and pennation angle fell by a large to very large amount. Weekly volumes ranged from about 21 to 73 repetitions with no clear volume trend. Studies of 4 weeks showed trivial to small change. Control groups showed trivial or negative change (g of 0.14 or less).",
   "limitations": "Only 13 studies, two without a control group; several studies had low TESTEX scores and did not report compliance or blinded assessment; the review was not pre-registered; the volume conclusion rests on uncontrolled pre-post effects.",
   "practicalImplications": "Protocols of 6 or more weeks produced large gains in the included studies, and volume did not clearly change the result. Where soreness drives poor adherence, a lower and consistent weekly volume may be a reasonable option, with intensity progressed over time.",
   "athleteDev": "Run NHE blocks for at least 6 weeks, progress the exercise's intensity rather than adding volume, and track compliance. A lower consistent volume may suit squads where soreness limits adherence.",
   "rtp": "The review contains no injured athletes and does not measure return to sport or injury outcomes. Strength and fascicle changes are surrogate outcomes for injury risk, so it cannot show that any NHE volume reduces re-injury or sets return-to-sport loads."
 }
}

 "confidence": "high",
 "studyDesign": "Randomized Controlled Trial",
 "primaryDomain": "Training & Performance",

 "sports": ["Soccer"],
 "populations": ["Male Athletes", "Healthy Athletes", "Youth / Adolescent"],
 "evidenceSummary": "Randomised trial of 20 U-20 male soccer players (22 enrolled, 2 withdrew for unrelated injury) assigned to a flywheel Romanian deadlift (n = 10) or a traditional Romanian deadlift (n = 10), twice weekly for 6 weeks alongside usual training, with no control group. Eccentric hamstring strength rose 13% (37 N, P = .03) in the flywheel group and 5% (14 N, P = .282) in the traditional group, while 3RM Romanian deadlift rose 18% (flywheel) and 28% (traditional), both P < .001; the group x time interaction was significant for 3RM (P = .02) but not for eccentric strength (P = .18).",
 "screeningLimitations": "Ten players per group, six weeks only, no control group, and no matched training history. The between-group test for eccentric strength was not significant, so a flywheel advantage is not established even though the within-group gain was.",
 "synthesisCaution": "Staff could read the flywheel group's significant eccentric gain as proof that flywheel RDL beats traditional RDL for hamstring strength, when the between-group interaction for eccentric strength was not significant (P = .18) and the traditional group gained more 3RM.",
 "paper": {
   "year": 2024,
   "citation": "O Brien J, Browne D, Earls D, Lodge C. The Effect of A Flywheel Hip Extension Vs A Traditional Hip Extension Exercise on Hamstring Strength. International Journal of Strength and Conditioning. 2024.",
   "doi": "10.47206/ijsc.v4i1.272",
   "abstract": "Twenty U-20 male soccer players did six weeks of either flywheel or traditional Romanian deadlift twice weekly. Both improved 3RM deadlift strength; only the flywheel group showed a significant gain in eccentric hamstring strength, and the authors describe its gain as superior.",
   "tldr": "In U-20 soccer players, six weeks of flywheel or traditional Romanian deadlift both raised 3RM strength. Only the flywheel version showed a significant eccentric hamstring gain, but the groups did not differ significantly on that outcome, so a flywheel advantage is not established.",
   "methods": "Random allocation to flywheel RDL (inertial load set by a power test; 4 sets of 6 with two extra submaximal pre-repetitions) or traditional RDL (80% of predicted 1RM), twice weekly for 6 weeks with matched set-RPE 8. Outcomes were 3RM RDL and peak eccentric NHE force on a Nordbord device before and after training, analysed with a 2 x 2 group x time repeated-measures ANOVA.",
   "findings": "Eccentric strength rose 13% (37 N, P = .03, g = 0.51) in the flywheel group but 5% (14 N, P = .282) in the traditional group; the time x group interaction for eccentric strength was not significant (P = .18). 3RM rose 18% (19 kg, g = 1.07) in the flywheel group and 28% (26 kg, g = 0.99) in the traditional group, with a significant time x group interaction (P = .02) favouring the traditional group's larger gain.",
   "limitations": "No control group, six weeks only, small groups, and usual training was not controlled. The abstract and discussion describe superior eccentric gains for flywheel, but the interaction test was not significant (P = .18). The text effect sizes (g = 0.51 and 1.07) also differ from Table 2 (d = 0.53 and 1.11).",
   "practicalImplications": "Either flywheel or traditional RDL can build 3RM Romanian deadlift strength in youth soccer players over 6 weeks. The flywheel version may add an eccentric hamstring gain, but this trial does not show that it is better than a traditional RDL for that outcome.",
   "athleteDev": "Either flywheel or traditional RDL can build hip extension strength in youth players. Use the flywheel version if an eccentric gain is the goal, with the caveat that the group difference was not significant, and match intensity with set-RPE.",
   "rtp": "Players were healthy and uninjured; no injured athletes and no return-to-play outcome were studied. It is a strength-block study, so it cannot set return-to-sport loads or show reduced re-injury."
 }
}
